\section{Evidence boundary, open problems, and conclusion}
\label{qua:sec:scope}

The quantum query bound follows from the analytic argument in
\cref{qua:sec:model,qua:sec:algorithm,qua:sec:correctness,qua:sec:complexity}; it does not
depend on computational verification.

\paragraph{Small proof-of-concept experiments.}
Appendix~\ref{qua:app:experiments} reports 5,000 ideal-sampler trials at
$K=3,N=16$, a separate 16-state Grover experiment, and exact finite
split-tree comparisons.  It describes the experimental settings and outcomes
directly.  These illustrate the recursion and sampler symmetry rather than
establishing a wall-clock or hardware speedup.

\paragraph{Use of AI tools.}
GPT-based tools (ChatGPT and Codex) supported brainstorming and constructive
discussion of the theoretical arguments and numerical experiments, as well
as manuscript polishing and review.

Two algorithmic questions remain.  First, determine whether a randomized
classical algorithm can match the
$\widetilde O(\sqrt M)$ upper bound; \cref{qua:prop:classical-lower} leaves a
large exponent gap.  Second, determine whether the implicit-set method can be
adapted to off-diagonal or hypergraph Ramsey total search, and whether the
multicolour bound in \cref{qua:cor:multicolour} can be sharpened by a scale-aware
estimator.

For the hypergraph question, quantum walks already give sublinear-query
algorithms for fixed sub-hypergraph containment
\cite{LeGallNishimuraTani2016}.  As a separate, speculative pointer,
higher-order symmetry representations have been useful in a different
hypergraph learning setting \cite{ZhangXinDey2024}.  Whether such structure can
be exposed with sublinear coherent queries in a Ramsey total-search problem is
open.

In summary, the constructive Ramsey recursion can be implemented without
materializing its exponentially shrinking candidate sets.  Capped uniform
search and a scale-aware error schedule give a
$\widetilde O(\sqrt N)$ query algorithm at the succinct Ramsey scale.  This
does not imply a new numerical Ramsey bound, a physical speedup, or a
quantum-versus-all-classical separation.
